title: Subscription Payment Plans
subtitle: One subscription, four ways to pay for it — upfront, monthly, free entry or a loan — across Razorpay, Stripe, PayU and cards. High-level and low-level design.
seoTitle: Design Subscription Payment Plans with Multiple Gateways (Real Interview Question, HLD + LLD)
description: A real interview question — design a subscription service with upfront, monthly, free and loan-based payment plans over multiple payment gateways, with both architecture and Java class design.
author: Editorial Team

blocks.text: **The question, as it was asked:** A user can subscribe to a service in 4 ways. Payment plan 1: pay upfront (one down payment). Payment plan 2: monthly subscription. Payment plan 3: backdoor entry, which is 0 payment. Payment plan 4: loan + a small entry fee, then loan installments. Gateways which can be used to pay: Razorpay, Stripe, PayU, card.
Understanding the Problem

blocks.title: What are we building?
blocks.text: The checkout and billing system behind a paid service — think an online program or premium membership — where the same subscription can be bought four different ways, and payments can go through several payment gateways. The interesting part isn't charging a card once; it's keeping **access** and **money** in sync over months of renewals, installments, failures and retries.

This prompt is short and could be asked as a high-level design round *or* a low-level (class design) round. This page covers both: the architecture first, then the classes and Java code. Start by stating your assumptions:
Assumptions

items: **Upfront** buys the full term (say 12 months) for one payment.
**Monthly** charges now, then automatically every month until cancelled.

**"Backdoor" entry (0 payment)** means access without paying: complimentary seats, partner or employee access, scholarships, promo codes. It skips the payment step, which makes it the plan most open to abuse.

**Loan** is financed by a partner lender (an NBFC or BNPL provider): the user pays a small **entry fee** now, the lender approves a loan and pays us, and the user repays the lender in **installments**. We don't lend money ourselves (that would need a lending licence).
**Gateways:** Razorpay, Stripe and PayU are full gateways. "Card" is a direct card processor integration. The user's card details never touch our servers — gateways give us tokens.
**Scale:** ~1M subscribers, peaks of a few hundred checkouts per second during sales. This is a **correctness** problem far more than a scale problem.

blocks.text: Functional Requirements
Core Requirements

items: Users should be able to choose a plan and check out.
Users should be able to pay through any supported gateway.
Access should follow payment status (activate, suspend, end).
Monthly charges and installments should be collected automatically.
Users should be able to finance a subscription with a loan.
Authorized staff should be able to grant 0-payment access.

blocks.text: Below the line (out of scope):

items: Tax calculation and invoice formatting.
Refund policies beyond the cases discussed.
The lender's own credit decisioning.

blocks.question: What are the non-functional requirements for this system?

blocks.text: Non-Functional Requirements
Core Requirements

items: **Money correctness:** never charge twice for the same thing, never lose a successful payment, and activate access exactly once.
**Resilience to gateway failures:** one gateway being slow or down must not stop people from subscribing.
**Extensibility:** adding a fifth gateway or a new plan type shouldn't mean rewriting checkout.
**Security and compliance:** no raw card data stored (PCI scope stays with the gateways), signed webhooks, auditable 0-payment grants.
**Auditability:** every money movement and every access change can be explained later.

blocks.text: Below the line (out of scope):

items: Sub-second checkout latency (a few seconds for a payment is normal).

lines: - never double charge, never lose a payment
- new plan / gateway = new class, not a rewrite
- no card data stored, audit everything
blocks.caption: Requirements on the whiteboard

blocks.text: The Set Up
Defining the Core Entities

items: **Plan:** id, type (`UPFRONT`, `MONTHLY`, `FREE`, `LOAN`), price, term, entry fee, installment count.
**Subscription:** user, plan, status (`PENDING`, `ACTIVE`, `PAST_DUE`, `SUSPENDED`, `CANCELLED`, `EXPIRED`), current access period.
**Scheduled charge:** subscription, amount, due date, purpose (`FULL`, `MONTHLY`, `ENTRY_FEE`), status.
**Payment attempt:** charge, gateway, gateway reference, idempotency key, status (`CREATED`, `PENDING`, `SUCCEEDED`, `FAILED`, `UNKNOWN`).
**Payment method / mandate:** a gateway token for a saved card or a recurring mandate (never the card number).
**Loan:** subscription, lender, amount, status (`APPLIED`, `APPROVED`, `DISBURSED`, `REPAYING`, `DEFAULTED`, `CLOSED`).
**Access grant:** for 0-payment access — who granted it, why, approved by whom, expiry.
**Ledger entry:** double-entry record of every money movement.

blocks.text: **Key insight:** every plan is just a different **payment schedule** — a list of charges over time.

rows: none for us (installments go to the lender)

blocks.text: Once you see that, the rest of the system — checkout, billing, access — doesn't care which plan it is.
API or System Interface

blocks.code:
GET  /v1/plans                                   -> Plan[]

POST /v1/subscriptions        Idempotency-Key: <uuid>
     { planId, gateway?: "razorpay" | "stripe" | "payu" | "card" }
     -> { subscriptionId, status, payment?: { attemptId, checkout: { redirectUrl | sdkParams } } }

GET  /v1/subscriptions/{id}                      -> Subscription (+ schedule)
POST /v1/subscriptions/{id}/cancel

POST /v1/webhooks/{gateway}                      (signed, from Razorpay/Stripe/PayU/card processor)
POST /v1/webhooks/lenders/{lender}               (loan approved / disbursed / defaulted)

POST /v1/grants               (staff only)  { userId, planId, reason, expiresAt }
POST /v1/grants/{id}/approve  (a second staff member)
POST /v1/redeem               { code }           (single-use promo codes)

blocks.text: The user comes from the auth token. The client never sends an amount — prices come from the plan on the server.
High-Level Design
1) Users should be able to choose a plan and check out

The **Subscription Service** reads the plan from a **Plan Catalog**, creates the subscription as `PENDING`, and asks the plan for its **payment schedule**. If something is due now, it hands that charge to the **Payment Orchestrator**; otherwise (free entry) it goes straight to activation checks. The `Idempotency-Key` on the request means a double-click or retry returns the same subscription instead of creating two.
2) Users should be able to pay through any supported gateway

The **Payment Orchestrator** creates a **payment attempt** and picks a gateway through a **router** (user's choice, payment method, currency, gateway health, cost). Each gateway sits behind the same **adapter** interface, so the orchestrator never contains Razorpay- or Stripe-specific code.

The gateway returns a checkout session (redirect URL or SDK parameters). The user pays on the gateway's page or SDK — card details go straight to the gateway, so we stay out of PCI scope. The gateway then calls our **webhook endpoint**; we verify the signature, look up the attempt by its gateway reference, and move it to `SUCCEEDED` or `FAILED`.
Never activate access because the browser was redirected to a "success" page — users can fake that URL. Only the gateway's signed webhook (or a server-side status check) is the truth.
3) Access should follow payment status

When a payment succeeds, the orchestrator records it and emits a `PaymentSucceeded` event (via an outbox). The Subscription Service consumes it, moves the subscription `PENDING → ACTIVE`, and an **Entitlement Service** grants access for the paid period. Products check entitlements with a fast cached lookup (`userId → active until`) instead of asking the payment system.
The subscription is a **state machine**, and every transition is explicit:

rows: Payment succeeded (or loan disbursed, or grant approved)
Retries exhausted after the grace period

blocks.text: Any transition not in the table is rejected — that's what stops a late "payment failed" webhook from cancelling a subscription that was already paid on retry.
4) Monthly charges and installments should be collected automatically

For monthly plans, the first checkout also creates a **recurring mandate** with the gateway (a saved token the gateway lets us charge later; in India, an RBI-compliant e-mandate). A **Billing Scheduler** stores future charges in a `scheduled_charges` table. Workers pick up charges that are due, charge the saved mandate through the same orchestrator, and update the subscription:

items: success → extend the access period;
failure → `PAST_DUE`, start **dunning** (retry after 1, 3 and 7 days, email the user to update their card), keep access during a short grace period, then `SUSPENDED`.

blocks.text: 5) Users should be able to finance a subscription with a loan

items: The user pays the **entry fee** through the normal checkout.
A **Loan Service** submits an application to the partner **lender** through a lender adapter (KYC and credit checks happen on the lender's side).
The lender approves and **disburses** the plan price to us; their webhook moves the loan to `DISBURSED` and the subscription to `ACTIVE`.
The user repays the lender in installments. The lender reports status to us; if the loan **defaults**, the contract decides what happens to access (commonly: suspend after a grace period).

blocks.text: If the lender **rejects** the application, the entry fee is refunded automatically (or kept, if the terms say it's a non-refundable processing fee — decide and say so). This is a small **saga**: each step has a compensating action.
6) Authorized staff should be able to grant 0-payment access
0-payment access never touches a gateway, so it needs its own controls instead:

items: Staff create an **access grant** with a reason and an expiry; a **second person approves** it (maker–checker) before access is activated.
Promo codes are **single-use**, expire, are tied to a campaign with a cap, and redemption is rate-limited per user and IP.
Every grant and redemption is written to an **audit log**, and finance gets a report of all free access.

blocks.text: Potential Deep Dives
1) How do we make sure a user is never charged twice and access is activated exactly once?

blocks.title: Trust the redirect and retry on failure

approach.text: Activate the subscription when the browser lands on the success page; if the gateway call times out, call it again.

challenges.text: Success URLs can be forged, users can close the tab before the redirect, and retrying after a timeout can charge the user twice because the first charge may have gone through.

approach.text: Each payment attempt has its own idempotency key that we send to the gateway, so a retry of the same attempt can't create a second charge. Access is activated from the signed webhook, not the redirect.

challenges.text: Webhooks can arrive twice, out of order, or before our own API call returns; a crash between "payment saved" and "subscription activated" can leave a paid user without access.

blocks.title: Payment state machine + unique gateway reference + outbox + reconciliation

items: Store every attempt with a **unique** `(gateway, gateway_reference)` and only allow forward state transitions (`PENDING → SUCCEEDED` happens once; a second `SUCCEEDED` webhook is a no-op).
Record webhook **event ids** with a unique constraint so duplicates are ignored.
Update the payment and write a `PaymentSucceeded` event to an **outbox** in the same transaction; the subscription is activated by consuming that event, idempotently.
Run **reconciliation** jobs: query gateways for attempts stuck in `PENDING`/`UNKNOWN`, and compare daily settlement reports against our ledger.

challenges.text: More tables and background jobs — but this is exactly what payment teams run. See [Payment Failure Scenarios](/learn/system-design/tips/payment-failure-scenarios) for the 21 failure cases this covers.

blocks.text: 2) What if a gateway is slow or down?

blocks.title: Retry the same payment on another gateway right away

approach.text: If Razorpay times out, immediately send the payment to Stripe instead.

challenges.text: A timeout means **unknown**, not failed. Razorpay may have charged the user, and now Stripe charges them again.

blocks.title: Health-based routing for new attempts, status checks for unknown ones

items: The router tracks each gateway's success rate and latency and puts a **circuit breaker** around each one; new checkouts go to healthy gateways.

An attempt that timed out is marked `UNKNOWN` and its status is **queried** from the same gateway before anything else happens. Only a definite failure lets the user retry, as a *new* attempt, possibly on another gateway.
Recurring charges use the gateway that holds the mandate; if it's down, the charge is retried later instead of switching gateways (mandates aren't portable).

challenges.text: Routing rules need care (some methods, like UPI or a particular card network, are only on some gateways), and reconciliation must cover every gateway.

blocks.text: 3) How do we run renewals and installments reliably?
The billing scheduler is a classic job-scheduler problem:

items: Charges live in a `scheduled_charges` table indexed by `due_at`. Workers claim due rows with `SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, so many workers run in parallel without picking the same charge.
Each scheduled charge id **is** the idempotency key for its payment, so a worker crash and retry can't charge twice.
Renewal runs are spread across the day (not all at midnight) to avoid gateway rate limits.
Dunning is just more scheduled charges with a retry policy, plus notifications.

blocks.text: 4) How do we stop abuse of the 0-payment route?

The 0-payment plan is the most likely place for losses, because no money changes hands to prove anything. Use maker–checker approval for staff grants, role-based permissions (only certain roles may grant, with per-person monthly caps), single-use expiring promo codes, alerts on unusual volumes (a staff member granting 200 seats in a day), and a regular review of active free subscriptions.
5) How do we keep the money records correct?

Use a **double-entry ledger**: every movement is recorded as entries that balance. For example, a user pays ₹12,000 upfront → debit *gateway receivable* ₹12,000, credit *deferred revenue* ₹12,000; when the gateway settles to our bank → debit *bank*, credit *gateway receivable*; each month of service delivered → debit *deferred revenue* ₹1,000, credit *revenue*. Never update balances in place. Daily **reconciliation** compares the ledger with each gateway's settlement report and the lender's statement, and flags mismatches for review.
Final Design
Low-Level Design
If this is asked as a class-design round, start from what will **change**, not from a list of patterns:

rows: Each plan is a class behind one interface that returns a payment schedule
New gateways, different SDKs and webhook formats
Each gateway is wrapped in a class behind one interface
A router picks an adapter by method, currency and health
Allowed transitions live in one place
Things that happen after activation (access, emails, analytics)

blocks.text: What **doesn't** change: the checkout flow and the subscription lifecycle. Those are the stable core that the swappable parts plug into.
The code (Java)
Extending it

rows: One new `PaymentGateway` class + register it. Checkout is untouched.
Add an annual plan or a 3-month free trial
New rule: suspend after 2 failed renewals instead of 3
Dunning policy config; the state machine stays the same.
Send a welcome email on activation

blocks.text: Which Standard Problems This Maps To

rows: Four plan types, including free and loan-financed
You're the *client* of several gateways, not the gateway
Ongoing access instead of a one-time order
Each job moves money, so idempotency is mandatory
The loan flow is a saga across you, the gateway and the lender

blocks.text: What's Different From the Textbook Version

items: **Multiple gateways.** Textbook payment questions have one processor. Here, routing, failover and "timeout = unknown" across providers are the interesting parts.
**Free and financed plans.** A plan with no payment needs authorization controls; a loan plan adds a third party and a saga.
**It doubles as an LLD question.** The four plans and four gateways are a textbook Strategy + Adapter setup — the interviewer may want classes, not boxes.

blocks.text: Follow-up Questions You May Get

rows: The user double-clicks Pay. What happens?
Idempotency key on checkout; the same subscription and attempt are returned
The gateway timed out — did the user pay?
Unknown: query the status (or wait for the webhook) before retrying anywhere
Money was deducted but the subscription isn't active
Webhook + outbox + reconciliation repair it; idempotent activation
The same webhook arrives three times
Unique event id; forward-only state transitions make repeats no-ops
Razorpay is down during a sale
Circuit breaker; route new checkouts to another gateway
The lender rejects the loan after the entry fee was paid
Compensating refund (or keep per terms) — a saga step
Do you store card numbers for monthly billing?
No — store the gateway's token/mandate; card data stays with the PCI-compliant gateway
The scheduled charge id is the idempotency key, and workers claim rows with `SKIP LOCKED`
A user upgrades from monthly to upfront mid-month
Prorate: credit unused days of the current period against the upfront price, then switch the schedule
Price per currency in the catalog; route to gateways that support the currency
How do you add PayPal next month?
One new adapter class + registration — show it in the LLD
How do you prevent staff from giving away free access?
Maker–checker approval, caps per role, audit log, anomaly alerts

blocks.text: Tips & Tricks for This Question

items: **Reframe the four plans as payment schedules** in the first few minutes. It turns a messy list of cases into one model, and interviewers notice.
**Ask early: HLD or LLD?** "Would you like me to focus on the services and data flow, or on the class design?" Then spend your time on the right thing.
**Treat "backdoor" carefully.** Say what you think it means (complimentary access) and immediately add controls — a 0-payment path without approval and audit is a red flag.
**Clarify who lends.** "I'll assume a partner lender pays us and collects installments" removes the whole credit-risk problem from your design, and shows judgment.
**Name "timeout = unknown"** whenever gateways come up. It's the single most important idea in payment interviews.
**In LLD, explain the force before the pattern:** "Gateways will keep changing, so each one sits behind an adapter" beats "I'll use the Adapter pattern".
**Don't** build your own card storage, let the client send the amount, or activate access from the success redirect.

quiz.question: What's the cleanest way to model the four payment plans?
options: A big if/else on plan type everywhere
Each plan produces a payment schedule behind one interface
quiz.explanation: Once every plan is a schedule of charges, checkout, billing and access don't need to know which plan it is.

quiz.question: Razorpay times out while charging a user. What should happen next?
options: Immediately charge the user on Stripe
Mark it failed and ask the user to pay again
Treat it as unknown and query Razorpay's status (or wait for the webhook) first
quiz.explanation: A timeout may hide a successful charge; switching gateways right away risks charging twice.

quiz.question: When should a subscription become ACTIVE after an online payment?
options: When the browser reaches the success page
When the gateway's signed webhook (or a server-side status check) confirms success
quiz.explanation: Redirects can be forged or lost; only the gateway's confirmation is trustworthy.

quiz.question: In the class design, which pattern lets you add a fifth gateway without touching checkout?
quiz.explanation: Each provider's SDK is wrapped in an adapter implementing the same interface; checkout only knows the interface.
